n: Ben-hadad II of Aram (Syria) besieges Samaria with a coalition of thirty-two vassal kings or chieftains. Israel’s capital is surrounded.

f.g: likely Ben-hadad II, king of Aram-Damascus; ‘son of (the god) Hadad.’
army.

n: He sends envoys into the city with his demands.
His demand is total: Ahab’s silver, gold, wives, and finest children belong to Ben-hadad.

f.g: the best, most attractive.

n: Ahab submits, treating it as a formal statement of vassal loyalty: “I am yours.”
Ben-hadad sends a second, harsher message, clarifying what he meant.
Now he will send men to search Ahab’s palace and the homes of his officials and take whatever they value. This is open humiliation and plunder.

f.g: precious to you.

n: Ahab consults the elders, pointing out that Ben-hadad is looking for trouble.

f.g: take note, pay attention.
harm, trouble.

n: The elders and people advise him to refuse.
Ahab agrees to the first terms but rejects the second.
Ben-hadad boasts that his army is so huge that Samaria’s dust wouldn’t give each soldier a handful—he will grind the city to powder.

f.w: The gods do so unto me, and more also
f.g: an oath formula: ‘May the gods punish me if I fail.’

n: Ahab answers with a proverb: a soldier putting on his armor shouldn’t boast like one taking it off after victory. In other words, don’t celebrate before the battle.

f.g: armor.

n: Ben-hadad, drinking with his allies in their tents, orders his troops into battle positions.

f.g: temporary shelters or booths.
take up battle positions.

n: Unexpectedly, a prophet comes to wicked Ahab with a promise of victory, so that Ahab will know the Lord is God. God’s mercy reaches even an unfaithful king.

f.w: thou shalt know that I am the LORD

n: The Lord will use the young officers of the district governors, and Ahab himself will lead the attack.

f.g: begin or lead the battle.
district governors.

n: Ahab’s forces are tiny: 232 young officers and 7,000 soldiers—the same number as the faithful remnant in chapter 19.
They attack at noon while Ben-hadad and his allies are drunk.
The young officers lead the way, and Ben-hadad’s scouts report them.
Overconfident, Ben-hadad orders them captured alive whether they come for peace or war.
The small force advances with the army behind it.
Each Israelite kills his opponent, the Arameans panic and flee, and Ben-hadad escapes on horseback.
Ahab joins the pursuit, striking the horses and chariots and winning a great victory.
The prophet warns Ahab to prepare, because Aram will attack again next spring, the season when kings went to war.

f.w: at the return of the year
f.g: next spring, the usual campaign season.

n: Ben-hadad’s advisers explain the defeat theologically: Israel’s gods must be mountain gods, so fight them on the plain. Ancient peoples often thought gods had limited territories.

f.g: many ancient peoples believed each god ruled a particular region.

n: They also advise replacing the vassal kings with professional military commanders.

f.g: in their places.

n: Rebuild an army equal to the one lost and fight on flat ground. Ben-hadad agrees.
The next spring Ben-hadad marches to Aphek, probably east of the Sea of Galilee, on level terrain.

f.g: a common place name; this one was likely east of the Sea of Galilee.

n: Israel’s army looks like two small flocks of goats compared to the Arameans, who fill the countryside.

f.g: young goats.

n: Because the Arameans claimed the Lord was only a god of the hills, He will give Israel the victory to prove He is God everywhere.

f.w: he is not God of the valleys

n: After a seven-day standoff, battle is joined and Israel strikes down a vast number of Aramean foot soldiers. Large numbers in ancient texts may reflect military units rather than exact counts.

f.g: infantry soldiers.

n: Survivors flee into Aphek, where a wall collapses on many more. Ben-hadad hides in an inner room.

f.g: literally ‘a room within a room,’ a hiding place.

n: Ben-hadad’s officials suggest begging for mercy, having heard Israel’s kings are merciful. They wear sackcloth and ropes as signs of surrender and submission.

f.g: coarse cloth worn in mourning or humility.
a sign of surrender, as captives with ropes on their necks.

n: They plead for Ben-hadad’s life. Ahab calls him “my brother”—a term for a treaty equal—shockingly friendly toward the enemy God had delivered to him.

f.g: treaty language for an ally of equal rank.

n: The servants seize on Ahab’s word as a hopeful sign. Ahab invites Ben-hadad into his royal chariot, a sign of honor.

f.g: quickly took it as an omen and held him to it.

n: Ben-hadad offers to return captured towns and grant Israel trading quarters in Damascus. Ahab makes a treaty and lets him go—putting political advantage ahead of God’s command.

f.w: make streets for thee in Damascus
f.g: set up market districts or trading quarters.

n: One of the “sons of the prophets”—members of a prophetic community—asks a companion, by the Lord’s word, to strike him. The companion refuses.

f.g: a fellowship or school of prophets, often led by Elijah or Elisha.

n: Because he refused a command given by the Lord’s word, a lion kills him—echoing the man of God in chapter 13. The story stresses that Ahab will be judged for his own disobedience.
Another man strikes the prophet and wounds him, as needed for the coming parable.
The prophet waits by the road disguised with a bandage over his eyes (or ashes) to look like a wounded soldier.

f.g: or ‘a bandage over his eyes’; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: He tells the king a made-up story: he was told to guard a prisoner on pain of death or a huge fine.

f.g: about 75 pounds of silver—far more than a soldier could pay.

n: While he was busy, the prisoner escaped. Ahab declares that the soldier has pronounced his own sentence—just as David did when Nathan told his parable.
The prophet removes his disguise and Ahab recognizes him.
The message: Ahab released a man the Lord had devoted to destruction, so Ahab’s own life will be forfeited, and his people will suffer. This is fulfilled in chapter 22.

f.g: Hebrew herem: devoted to God, under the ban.

n: Ahab returns to Samaria sullen and angry—not repentant. The same words describe him in the next chapter.

f.g: sullen and resentful.
